summary:
MIZRAK is a smart agriculture platform that transforms NASA climate data into practical farming decisions.

Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, MIZRAK leverages NASA POWER climate datasets, local soil conditions, and crop requirements to help farmers adapt to climate variability, improve crop planning, and optimize resource use.
Instead of overwhelming users with complex scientific information, MIZRAK delivers clear, actionable insights through an intuitive dashboard, enabling farmers to evaluate field conditions, explore suitable crop-rotation strategies, and make data-driven decisions with confidence.
By making space-based climate intelligence accessible and useful at the local level, MIZRAK empowers agricultural communities to build resilience, enhance sustainability, and prepare for the challenges of a changing climate.
MIZRAK: Turning NASA Data into Smarter Farming Decisions.
details:
MIZRAK: From Space to Soil, From Data to Decisions

Team KarakTech | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

1. Why we built this

Farming in Jordan is getting harder. In the Jordan Valley especially, water is scarce, summers are hotter, and rainfall is less predictable than it used to be. Farmers feel these changes first, but the scientific data that describes them is usually locked behind technical formats and tools that most people do not have time to learn.

MIZRAK is our attempt to close that gap. It is a web platform that takes NASA Earth observation data and presents it in a form that a farmer, a student, or an agricultural officer can read and use.

2. Study area

Our study region is the Jordan Rift Valley, from its northern end down past the southern shore of the Dead Sea. We defined it as a four-corner polygon on the map. The region combines intensive irrigated agriculture in the northern and central valley with extreme heat, very low rainfall, and the lowest land elevation on Earth near the Dead Sea. Because the valley is long, its climate and land use change noticeably from north to south, and we treat this as a central challenge of the project.

3. How the website works

The user starts by telling the website where the farm is, since every NASA dataset is tied to a specific location on Earth. The user then adds basic details about the farm: its area, soil type, water source, and the crops grown or planned.

With the location set, the website requests climate and solar data for those coordinates from the NASA POWER API and turns the response into charts and indicators that can be explored. Our long-term goal is to support crop planning, seasonal decisions, and water awareness. Guidance of that kind must combine satellite data with local soil knowledge and real agricultural experience, so we treat it as the direction we are growing toward, not as something we have finished.

4. NASA data: what we used and where its limits are

NASA POWER is integrated and is the data source our prototype relies on today. It provides air temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, wind, and other meteorological values for any location and time range. POWER is gridded data built from models and satellite processing. It describes the area around a farm. It is not a sensor reading from a specific field.

MODIS NDVI was obtained through NASA AppEEARS (MOD13Q1, version 061, 250 m resolution, 16-day composites) for a single point in the central Jordan Valley at 32.318°N, 35.570°E. We requested the first two weeks of November (1–13) of each year from 2000 to 2025. This produced 26 readings, one per year, and 22 of them passed the quality check. Values range from about 0.12 to 0.17. They are low, and we believe the reason is the timing of the readings, which fall after the summer crop harvest and before winter crops develop. We have not yet verified that explanation with a farmer or an agricultural advisor. The file contains no 2026 reading. Because every reading comes from the same two weeks each year, it supports comparing years with one another, not following a crop through a growing season. The point lies in the northern part of the study region and does not represent the whole polygon. The file is not yet integrated automatically with each farm’s data.

HLS (Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2, version 2.0) combines Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2 observations at 30 m resolution. Its data becomes available roughly two to three days after acquisition. AppEEARS offers ready-made vegetation-index products from HLS, so NDVI does not need to be computed separately.

SMAP L4 (SPL4SMGP) provides soil moisture at 9 km resolution every three hours, including surface soil moisture (0–5 cm) and an estimate for the root zone (0–100 cm). The root-zone value comes from a land model constrained by satellite observations and is not a direct measurement. A single grid cell is wider than the valley in many places, so a value describes the general area, not one farm.

GPM IMERG (Final Run, version 07) provides daily precipitation at 0.1° resolution, roughly 10 km. The Final Run is corrected after all satellite data is collected, so it arrives with a delay of about four months. Satellite precipitation estimates are less accurate near coasts and in complex terrain, and the Dead Sea basin has both.

5. Where we are today

Data source

Status

NASA POWER

Integrated and working

MODIS NDVI

File obtained for one trial point; not yet integrated per farm

HLS, SMAP, GPM IMERG

Retrieval scripts prepared for NASA Earthdata; under testing, results not yet confirmed

ECOSTRESS, SRTM

Not available; stated openly in the website

The website includes a section titled “Not available in this study” that lists each source we have not activated and gives the reason. For example, SMAP needs Earthdata authorization and quality-flag processing, ECOSTRESS needs product selection and quality screening, and SRTM needs elevation tiles to be downloaded, which is why the site uses GPS elevation instead. We chose not to display any number whose real source we do not have.

6. Technical challenges we faced

  • Accounts and approvals. Most of this NASA data requires an Earthdata account. GPM data additionally requires the user to accept the GES DISC archive terms from their own account, which only becomes visible on the first download attempt. We store credentials as protected secrets and never in code.
  • Different spatial scales. HLS is 30 m, MODIS is 250 m, SMAP is 9 km, and GPM is about 10 km. We do not compare their values directly, and we explain what each source can and cannot represent.
  • Different delays. POWER is close to real time, HLS lags by days, and IMERG Final lags by months. Some indicators describe the present, others describe the recent past, and we say so.

7. Limitations of this study

  • No team member has visited a farm or spoken with a farmer in the Jordan Valley. Our work so far rests on satellite data alone.
  • No agricultural advisor or farmer has reviewed our results. We therefore present them as environmental information for exploration and planning, not as ready-to-use agricultural recommendations.
  • We have not compared the satellite data with field measurements. The indicators describe the surrounding area, not an individual field.
  • A single NDVI point cannot represent the full length of the valley, and SMAP and GPM cells near the Dead Sea can mix land, water, and mountains.

8. Design

We wanted MIZRAK to feel simple. Navigation is plain, information is grouped in a sensible order, and charts are meant to be read at a glance by someone with no scientific training. Our visual identity draws on both fields we connect, with farmland and environmental imagery alongside space themes.

9. A side project: farming on Mars

We also built an educational simulation about growing food on Mars. It looks at what makes the planet hostile to agriculture: the cold, the thin atmosphere, the lack of liquid water, and the need for sealed, controlled growing spaces. It exists to spark curiosity and to link the problems farmers face on Earth with those future space missions will face. It is not a claim that crops can be grown on Mars today.

10. How we built it and who did what

We built the website in Replit and used Python where needed. NASA POWER supplies the live data, and NASA Earthdata and AppEEARS are where we find and download the other datasets.

Our team leader came up with the idea, set the direction, and supervised the work. Our programmer reviewed the code during development, checked the implementation, and caught technical problems. Our graphic designer created the visuals and the project identity. AI tools supported parts of the work, including some visual content and the preparation of data-retrieval scripts. The concept, the technical decisions, and the design choices were made by the team.

11. Next steps and intended impact

We plan to validate our results by reaching out to farmers and agricultural advisors in the region, and to add local soil data and data from the Ministry of Agriculture and the Jordan Valley Authority when they become available. We also plan to replace the single NDVI point with several points, or a polygon-based request, so that north, center, and south of the valley are each represented.

Our aim is to help farmers and communities in water-stressed regions make better-informed decisions. In the near term, that means easier access to climate information and a clearer picture of local patterns. As we add datasets, it should also mean a better view of vegetation, soil moisture, and rainfall changes. Longer term, we want to deepen the agricultural analysis, build real tools for crop planning and monitoring, and take what we learn in the Jordan Valley to other regions.
